data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"A test constrains its subject, rather than describing it, exactly when the subject's code path is installed before the test's oracle is allowed to fail on it \u2014 the 'shown-to-fail-first' installation ritual turns a description of intended behavior into a guard that binds future mutations.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the 1/9 compile.py mutation loss is shown to occur in a module without any pre-installed failing test, the installation mechanism is confounded.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If a control condition with fail-first installation reversed (pass-first) yields the same 3/26 distribution, the constraining effect is not installation-specific.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If all three surviving mutations are in modules with no ordinarily-guarded registry entries, the guard coverage story collapses.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the record shows the 3/26 were proposed by models that had not read the acceptance record, the planted-failure interpretation is weakened.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Under shown-to-fail-first installation, the failing test is planted in the registry as an already-failed expectation before the subject code is admitted. Compile.py's mutation pass then treats any mutation that would flip that pre-planted failure back to passing as a regression against the registry, so the test no longer reports what the code does but what the registry has committed the code must do. The 3-of-26 result is the surviving residue of mutations that alter declared data rather than added behavior \u2014 exactly the kind of change a pre-installed oracle cannot see because the oracle's failure was bound to the behavior, not the declaration.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
